body:
READING THE DEPRESSION IN NUMBERS (lesson)
1. From 3 percent (1929) to 25 percent (1933), an increase of 22 percentage points; about one worker in four.
2. Unemployment fell from 25 percent (1933) to 14 percent (1937), then rose to 19 percent (1938). Strong answers connect the rise to spending cuts and tighter credit in 1937.
3. Unemployment fell from 15 percent (1940) to 1 percent (1944) as federal war spending soared and millions joined the armed forces.
4. A drop from about 381 to about 41 is a loss of about 89 percent ((381 - 41) / 381 = 0.89). Strong answers note that few Americans owned stock but bank failures hurt ordinary savers directly.
5. Strong answers use the evidence: unemployment fell substantially under the New Deal but stayed above 14 percent until 1941; full employment came with the war. Some may argue the New Deal's reforms (FDIC, Social Security) mattered more than recovery.

FEAR ITSELF AND FOUR FREEDOMS (assignment)
Sourcing: inaugural address to a frightened nation in March 1933, meant to restore confidence; annual message to Congress in January 1941, meant to build support for aiding Britain.
Context: bank closures and 25 percent unemployment; by 1941 war in Europe and Asia, Lend-Lease debate.
Claim: strong answers argue Roosevelt expanded the idea of freedom from freedom from government (speech, worship) to include economic security ("freedom from want") and peace ("freedom from fear"), and made the federal government responsible for putting "people to work." Evidence: at least two quotations.
Corroboration: New Deal laws (WPA, Social Security), Roosevelt's 1944 call for an "economic bill of rights," critics who saw the New Deal as government overreach.

A GRAVE INJUSTICE (assignment)
Sourcing: an executive order of February 1942 stating a security justification and never naming Japanese Americans; a law passed by Congress in 1988 after a commission reviewed wartime records.
Context: Pearl Harbor (December 1941), long-standing anti-Asian prejudice and laws on the West Coast, wartime fear; by 1988, the civil rights movement and decades of Japanese American activism for redress.
Claim: strong answers explain that the 1942 order claimed "military necessity" while the 1988 findings concluded the removal had no adequate security basis and was "motivated largely by racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership." They explain the different perspectives of 1942 and 1988 and connect to Debs and Schenck.
Corroboration: Korematsu v. United States (1944); the commission's 1983 report; no Japanese American was convicted of espionage or sabotage during the war; about two-thirds of those removed were citizens.

DID THE NEW DEAL END THE DEPRESSION? (assessment)
Strong essays take a position and use the data: the New Deal brought unemployment down from 25 to 14 percent and reformed banking (FDIC: bank failures nearly stopped after 1933) and created Social Security, but unemployment stayed high and rose again in 1937-1938 after spending cuts; full recovery came with wartime spending after 1941. Many historians and economists conclude the New Deal relieved suffering and reformed institutions but did not by itself restore full employment. The best essays explain the policy lesson of 1937-1938 (fiscal and monetary tightening) and address a counterclaim.

Scoring tip: an essay that says only "the war ended the Depression" without data earns Developing on Historical evidence; Proficient requires at least two specific figures from the data reading used accurately.
title: Answer key: Depression and the Second World War
